title: Rep. Elgin Rogers, Jr. voted Nay on HB472, a bill waiving fees for identification and vital records for individuals experiencing homelessness
text:
Rep. Elgin Rogers, Jr. voted Nay on HB472, a bill waiving fees for identification and vital records for individuals experiencing homelessness
Rep. Elgin Rogers, Jr. (D-42nd) voted Nay on HB472, a bill waiving fees for identification and vital records for individuals experiencing homelessness, which passed the Ohio House 60-34 during the 136th Ohio General Assembly on Wednesday, June 10, 2026, according to the Ohio Legislature.
The following summary and breakdown are based on the bill's official text and may include interpretation to clarify the bill's provisions.
This bill waives state and local fees for certified copies of birth records, birth certificate certifications, and birth certificate replacements, as well as Ohio identification cards, for individuals experiencing homelessness. It defines who qualifies as experiencing homelessness, including people in shelters, in unsafe housing due to violence, or recently released from institutions without housing. To receive fee waivers, individuals must provide verification from specified officials such as social service agency directors, school staff, TRIO or GEAR UP directors, or college financial aid administrators.
HB472 was introduced by Jodi Salvo.
Rogers is the State Representative for Ohio House District 42, having been re-elected on November 5th, 2024. He was sworn into office on January 1, 2025, by Ohio Supreme Court Justice Melody J. Stewart Ph.D., who is noted for being the first African American woman elected across all counties in Ohio.
Rogers holds a Master of Arts degree from Indiana University, Bloomington, and a Bachelor of Arts degree from Kent State University.
Rogers also completed the Senior Executives in State and Local Government program at Harvard University Kennedy School and has a background in education, having researched and taught American Government and Political Science at the collegiate level.
In Ohio, the legislative process begins when a bill is introduced in either the House of Representatives or the Senate. A bill must receive three considerations in each chamber, and it may be referred to a committee for hearings, debate and possible amendments before advancing to a floor vote. If both chambers pass the same version, the bill is sent to the governor, who can sign it, veto it or allow it to become law without a signature. The Ohio General Assembly begins a new legislative session every two years on the first Monday in January of odd-numbered years, and there is no limit on the number of days it may convene.
